ai.definition: Neuromorphic computing is a computational paradigm that mimics the structure and function of the human brain to enable highly efficient and parallel processing.
ai.howItWorks: By designing hardware architectures inspired by biological neural networks, neuromorphic systems can process information in a manner similar to how neurons operate in the brain. This includes features such as event-driven computing, where data is processed only when changes occur, and spiking neural networks that mimic the firing of individual neurons.
ai.problemSolved: It addresses the limitations of traditional von Neumann architectures by providing more efficient and scalable solutions for complex tasks like pattern recognition, learning, and decision-making in real-time scenarios.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing neuromorphic chips involves advanced semiconductor fabrication techniques to integrate transistors that can mimic neural behavior. This includes the use of memristive devices and other emerging technologies.
ai.buildProcess: The build process starts with designing the architecture, followed by prototyping using specialized software tools. Then, it moves on to fabricating the hardware at semiconductor facilities before testing and validation.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the complexity of the design, the need for advanced fabrication processes, and the integration of emerging materials and technologies.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is positive but faces challenges in standardization and widespread adoption.
ai.regulation: Regulations are still evolving. There may be concerns around data privacy and security due to the nature of neuromorphic systems.
ai.risks: Technological risks include the complexity of designing and validating neuromorphic systems, while market risks involve the need for significant investment in infrastructure and training.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain given the current stage of development and limited commercial applications. However, potential long-term benefits could lead to significant market opportunities.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may include advancements in materials science, integration with other AI technologies, and improvements in energy efficiency.

glossary.def: Relating to or inspired by the structure and function of biological neural networks.
A computational model that mimics how neurons in the brain communicate via spikes (or action potentials).
A paradigm where data processing occurs only when specific events or changes are detected, as opposed to continuous processing.

subsystems.name: Spiking neuron circuits
subsystems.role: mimic biological neurons: they accumulate input and emit a spike only when a threshold is crossed.

subsystems.name: Synaptic array
subsystems.role: stores connection weights locally, so computation and memory sit together.

subsystems.name: Event-driven interconnect
subsystems.role: routes spikes as asynchronous packets only when a neuron fires, saving power.

subsystems.name: Learning and plasticity engine
subsystems.role: adjusts weights using local rules such as spike-timing-dependent plasticity.

subsystems.name: Sensory front-end
subsystems.role: converts real-world signals into sparse spike trains.

subsystems.name: Software stack
subsystems.role: maps neural networks onto the hardware and simulates them.

buildSteps.title: Choose a neuron model
buildSteps.detail: Pick a simple, hardware-friendly spiking model such as leaky integrate-and-fire, then design its analog or digital circuit.

buildSteps.title: Design the synapse
buildSteps.detail: Select a weight-storage technology — memristor, phase-change memory or SRAM — and lay out a dense crossbar array.

buildSteps.title: Lay out a tile
buildSteps.detail: Combine a group of neurons, their synapses and a router into a repeating tile that can be tiled across the chip.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the chip
buildSteps.detail: Use standard CMOS for logic and signalling; if memristors are used, add them in the back-end-of-line above the transistors.

buildSteps.title: Test and calibrate
buildSteps.detail: Measure spiking behaviour across many neurons and compensate for device-to-device variability with calibration.

buildSteps.title: Train and map the network
buildSteps.detail: Train the network (often off-chip with conventional deep-learning tools), then compile its weights onto the synaptic array.

buildSteps.title: Integrate into a system
buildSteps.detail: Pair the chip with event-based sensors and a host processor to run always-on inference in a real device.

prerequisites.tech: Non-volatile memory with analog weight storage
prerequisites.why: memristors and phase-change cells can hold weights densely and cheaply, but their variability and endurance are still being improved.
cameras that output spikes only when pixels change are commercially available and naturally match neuromorphic hardware.
spiking chips avoid a global clock, so they need proven network-on-chip and handshaking techniques.
local rules like STDP work in small demos but scaling them to large, accurate tasks remains an open research problem.

pathway.milestone: research chips and large-scale spiking machines demonstrate real-time spiking neural networks
pathway.unlocks: ultra-low-power always-on vision and robotics prototypes.

pathway.milestone: hybrid systems that combine neuromorphic cores with conventional processors
pathway.unlocks: practical edge devices for keyword spotting, gesture recognition and anomaly detection.

pathway.milestone: commercial chips with on-chip learning and memristor crossbars
pathway.unlocks: adaptive sensors and devices that learn locally without sending data to the cloud.

pathway.milestone: large-scale brain-inspired architectures for cognitive computing
pathway.unlocks: new AI workloads that today's deep learning handles poorly, such as continual learning and sparse reasoning.
